name: Life Transitions
title: Your life has changed. You do not have to have the next part figured out.
summary: A transition can bring opportunity, loss, relief, and uncertainty together. Explore the practical and emotional parts of change, without being asked to turn every ending into a positive story.
cardSummary: Read about the gap between an external change and feeling settled in it. Explore a fictional career-transition example, the difference between solving a practical problem and living with uncertainty, and ways to define a useful starting conversation.

panel.title: You can choose a change and still find it difficult.
paragraphs: A new job, a move, a relationship ending, a changed health need, or a different family role does not have to be entirely good or bad. The first task can be making room for the actual experience.

items.title: Separate the questions
items.text: What changed outside, and what changed for you?

items.title: Read a transition example
items.text: A promotion arrives before a sense of belonging does.

sections.title: A change in circumstances can ask more than one kind of work of you.
paragraphs: Change can involve uncertainty about routines, relationships, expectations, and the future. NHS guidance on managing change emphasizes noticing how you feel, focusing on manageable short-term needs, maintaining useful connections, and getting practical advice when a problem calls for it.

For a therapy conversation, it can help to separate the event from its meaning. A move is an event; losing familiar people or wondering where you belong may be part of the experience. A promotion is an event; questioning whether you can still be yourself in a new role is another question.

This guide does not treat a difficult adjustment as an automatic diagnosis. Nor does it require you to become grateful for something you did not choose. You can explore loss, pressure, possibility, or uncertainty without settling the story before seeking support.

panel.title: Not knowing yet is different from having no way forward.
paragraphs: You may not be ready for a life plan. A useful conversation can focus on the next decision, the support you need, or what deserves time before you act.

sections.title: What has become unfamiliar?
sections.intro: These are illustrative questions, not stages you must complete.

items.title: Your routines
items.teaser: The old ways of getting through a week no longer fit.
paragraphs: A familiar routine may have depended on a place, relationship, schedule, or ability that has changed. You can discuss which parts still support you and which now create unnecessary friction.
The question is not how quickly you can reproduce the old week. It is what would make the current one more workable, including support that cannot be supplied by personal discipline alone.

items.title: Your role
items.teaser: Others see the new title before you feel comfortable inside it.
paragraphs: Becoming a parent, ending a caregiving role, changing careers, or living alone can raise questions about what you are responsible for and what gives the day meaning.
An inquiry can leave room for both attachment to the old role and curiosity about the next one. You do not have to reject your past to consider a different future.

items.title: Your decisions
items.teaser: Every choice feels connected to an uncertain bigger picture.
paragraphs: Sometimes one decision is being asked to resolve everything: where to live, what a relationship means, or whether a new direction will work. A practical conversation can separate decisions that must be made now from questions that can remain open.
When a choice needs legal, financial, medical, or other specialized advice, therapy should not replace that expertise. Emotional support and practical advice can serve different purposes.

sections.title: The promotion is good news. Monday still feels unsettling.
sections.intro: A fictional example about a chosen change with mixed meanings.

items.title: What changed
paragraphs: Noor accepts a promotion they worked toward. The new role changes the schedule, relationships with colleagues, and expectations about decisions.

items.title: What feels difficult
paragraphs: Noor misses being part of the old team and worries that admitting uncertainty will look ungrateful. They keep trying to decide whether the promotion was a mistake.

items.title: What could be separated
paragraphs: A therapist might help Noor distinguish missing a familiar role, needing clearer information, and evaluating whether the new work fits. Those questions do not need the same answer or the same timetable.

reveal.title: Why not simply focus on the positive?
paragraphs: In this example, gratitude would not answer the practical questions about expectations or replace the relationships Noor misses. A fuller conversation can include what is welcome, what is lost, and what needs more information.

A useful next step might be a clarification at work, a discussion of boundaries, or more time to observe the new routine. The example does not promise that a difficult transition will become the right choice; it shows how not to force one feeling to settle every question.

sections.kicker: Give each question the right kind of attention
sections.title: Some problems need action. Some uncertainty needs room.

items.title: A practical problem
paragraphs: An unanswered question about a schedule, access to care, a responsibility, or an agreement may call for information or concrete help. Reflection alone may not resolve it.

items.title: An experience still taking shape
paragraphs: You may be grieving a familiar life, rethinking a role, or not yet know what you prefer. Pressure for an immediate positive conclusion can hide the question rather than answer it.

sections.kicker: Make the next step smaller than the whole future
sections.title: Start with what needs attention this week.

items.title: Describe the change
paragraphs: Name the event and what is different in an ordinary day. Include what you chose, what you did not choose, and what remains unclear.

items.title: Identify the competing needs
paragraphs: There may be a need for stability alongside a wish for change, or relief alongside grief. You can discuss both without treating one as the correct response.

items.title: Choose a useful question
paragraphs: A first goal could be understanding a decision, making a week more manageable, or discussing a relationship affected by the transition. Keep it connected to your actual circumstances.

items.title: Review what you learn
paragraphs: New information may change the plan. Decide with the clinician how you will revisit goals and whether other support or assessment is needed.

sections.title: Support does not require a crisis or a completed plan.

items.question: Can therapy help with a change I chose?
paragraphs: You can seek support around the demands, uncertainty, or mixed feelings of a chosen change. The first inquiry can describe what you are finding difficult without treating the decision as a failure.

items.question: What if other people think I should be happy?
paragraphs: You can bring the difference between their interpretation and your experience into the conversation. The goal is not to decide whose feelings are permitted; it is to understand what the change means for you.

items.question: Will a therapist make the decision for me?
paragraphs: You can ask for help clarifying priorities, patterns, information gaps, and options. The working agreement should make room for your choices rather than require the therapist's preferred outcome.

items.question: What if this feels more serious than ordinary adjustment?
paragraphs: Describe persistent changes in mood, sleep, anxiety, or functioning to a health professional. A transition does not rule out another condition or the need for more support. A clinician can assess that rather than assume everything is explained by change.
